facts.claim: Taiwan's Uniform Invoice Lottery links prize eligibility to retaining an official sales receipt.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because customers request and keep invoices for the drawing, so merchants face more pressure to record taxable sales.
facts.commonError: The lottery rewards merchants for voluntarily reporting revenue.
facts.whyWrong: The consumer's demand for an official invoice is the enforcement lever.

facts.claim: Beijing's 2002 restaurant receipt lottery used scratch-off prizes on official invoices.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because an immediate chance to win made diners more likely to request the document that registers the sale.
facts.commonError: The policy reduced tax evasion by raising restaurant fines at checkout.
facts.whyWrong: Its distinctive mechanism was a customer reward rather than a larger penalty.

facts.claim: Hyde Park bookstores and the Concord Bookshop compete through curated selection even though they cannot match Amazon's catalog size.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because human judgment and physical arrangement reduce search burden while creating discovery and trust.
facts.commonError: A smaller inventory always produces a strictly worse choice experience.
facts.whyWrong: Selection can add informational value when the curator's taste is useful.

facts.claim: Navigation and curation address different forms of choice overload.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because navigation helps locate a known target, whereas curation decides which unfamiliar options deserve attention.
facts.commonError: A better search box makes editorial selection unnecessary.
facts.whyWrong: Search cannot retrieve an option the chooser does not know to seek.

facts.claim: Tom Sawyer makes fence painting desirable by presenting access to the task as scarce and enjoyable.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the reframing changes the social meaning from imposed labor to a privilege others must earn.
facts.commonError: The fence scene motivates helpers with higher wages.
facts.whyWrong: The reward is perceived exclusivity and play, not cash.

facts.claim: A reward can motivate more effectively when it feels like a guilt-free pleasure rather than fungible cash.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a designated treat avoids the mental-accounting pressure to spend ordinary money on necessities.
facts.commonError: Only the monetary face value of a reward affects behavior.
facts.whyWrong: Label and form alter how recipients experience and use the reward.

facts.claim: Frequent-flier rewards and coffee punch cards convert repeated transactions into visible progress.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because accumulating status or stamps supplies immediate feedback before the final reward arrives.
facts.commonError: Loyalty programs work only by cutting the unit price.
facts.whyWrong: Progress, status, and earmarked treats can motivate beyond a cash-equivalent discount.

facts.claim: A playful nudge can change behavior without changing the underlying requirement or banning alternatives.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because it adds an attractive experience or symbolic payoff to the desired action.
facts.commonError: Any use of prizes is a mandate.
facts.whyWrong: Participation remains optional when the original alternatives stay available.

facts.claim: Curation creates value only when the selector's judgment is credible to the chooser.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a reduced menu helps when exclusions carry useful information rather than arbitrary limitation.
facts.commonError: Removing options automatically improves every large menu.
facts.whyWrong: A bad curator can discard valuable options and impose irrelevant taste.

allowedAnchors.label: fun and curation
allowedAnchors.text: Curation reduces a large universe to a purposeful selection, while fun supplies an intrinsic or symbolic reward for participation. People are more likely to engage when design offers discovery, pleasure, or a memorable reward instead of another obligation.
